paragraphs.text: Above is a Buisness Insider Article Titled “7 things to know about carbon capture and storage technology” which is sponsored by Exxon Mobil. It argues that carbon capture and storage (CCS) is a crucial, proven method for cutting CO₂ in power generation and manufacturing sectors that can work alongside renewables for work towards to climate goals. It highlights ExxonMobil’s CCS infrastructure development and research into technologies like direct air capture and advanced materials, and geologic storage capacity. Overall, it states CCS (often paired with natural gas) as essential for achieving large-scale emissions reductions.

Running this article through Augmented CARDS classifies the article as ‘Not Contrarian', with a score of 0.9995488524436951. This is reasonable as the article does not disagree with climate change, its seriousness or its impacts and in fact actively supports the common climate discourse. Removing the binary classifier from Augmented CARDS, this article, like majority of the other in our dataset, is categorised in a level 4 claim: Climate Solutions won’t Work. In particular for this article the level 4 sublabel is Clean energy technology/biofuels won’t work. This categorisation had a score of 0.9398143291473389, which again logically makes sense as the article is framing renewable energies and insufficient by themselves as the requirement for CCS programs like Exxon Mobil’s. This demonstrates how Augmented CARDS works well; however, is not adequate for detecting the kind of native advertising rhetoric used in the article.

Running this article through CLAIMS gives the following binary labels as true: green_decreasing_emissions, green_false_solutions, and green_generic_environmental_references for green labels and ff_primary_product and ff_infrastructure_and_production and fossil fuel labels. These green labels were reasoned due to the post’s advocation of CCS as a central decarbonization technology (a false solution), the mention of lower-emission futures (green messaging), and references to the Paris Agreement and broad climate contexts (generic environmental references). The fossil fuel labels were derived due to explict mentions of fossil fuels and natural gas infrastructure as well as the and production context via the ExxonMobil CCS hub. green_viable_solutions, green_recycling_waste_management, green_nature_animal_references and ff_petrochemical_product were all false as there was no explicit mention of recycling/waste managemenat content, animals, clear corporate policies beyond general climate discourse and any petrochemical products.
These labels align with the native advert discourse present in the article’s content demonstrating CLAIMS’ appropriateness for this type of article.

paragraphs.text: Climate action and native advertising: How fossil fuel companies position their sincerity in American and British news media
Abstract:

Confronting severe economic challenges in the twenty-first century, many news media are experimenting with new relationships with advertisers, including the focus of this study: native advertising. At the same time, as the climate crisis worsens, and political pressures and news coverage increase, we are seeing the fossil fuel industry expand and shift its communication about the topic. This study sits at the intersection of these trends: we ask to what extent, and how, native advertisements are being employed in fossil fuel communication campaigns. We analyze 252 native ads sponsored by fossil fuel companies between 2014 and 2022 in leading English-language news outlets. Led by human quantitative content analysis, with supplementary automated text analysis, we show that the style of climate science denial documented by, e.g., Oreskes and Supran (2011), is absent from native ad communications; in its place are frequent mentions of the environment, the reality of climate change, and the need to decarbonize. In fact, the primary position of fossil fuel companies in our data is the assertion that they are leading the decarbonization of energy systems. To do so, they strongly emphasize the relative virtues of natural gas and promote investments in unproven new technologies. A secondary tactic emphasizes the importance of energy to development and quality of life. Our discussion explores the challenges of analyzing claims that are often superficially true but misleading in context and the questions misleading native advertising raises for news media facing a challenging digital media landscape.
Keywords:
advertising, climate change, environment, disinformation, fossil fuels
INTRODUCTION

The intertwining of news content with corporate promotions has a long history, particularly in the United States. And the fossil fuel industry has often been an innovator in developing techniques for bringing its messages as close as possible to journalistic news. Indeed, starting during the first American oil crisis, between 1972 and 1985, Mobil Oil purchased weekly space (sometimes more frequently) in the opinion section of The New York Times and other newspapers. As Murphree and Aucoin (2010) relate, the move was audacious for its insertion of corporate messaging directly into the opinion section of a newspaper, as opposed to product advertising in other sections; and such messages came to be known as “advertorials,” reflecting the mixing of paid content with the physical space, form, and format of newspapers’ venerable editorials (Brown, Waltzer and Waltzer 2001). Facing criticism related to record company profits during the oil shortage, Mobil was explicitly battling news media and politicians over “who would set the agenda for public debate on energy policy” (Murphree and Aucoin 2010: 7).

The move was a logical one in the practice of public relations—and the past five decades has seen continued development of the suite of strategies now known as “information and influence campaigns,” including efforts to obtain favorable news coverage and direct buying of space in news outlets. They are now essential to many large companies’ efforts to maintain legitimacy and “social license to operate” (Harvey and Bice 2014; Manheim 2011).

For news organizations, acceptance of sponsored content is more fraught. The combination of declining revenue from classified and traditional advertising, and the eagerness of companies to reach audiences with “integrated” messaging give news outlets clear incentives to support their bottom lines with a wide array of sponsorship types. But it is well known that most readers do not distinguish integrated advertising from genuine news and are distrustful of it when they do; and most journalists and advertisers consider the practice generally deceptive (Amazeen and Wojdynski 2020; Schauster, Ferrucci and Neill 2016).

Further, sponsoring companies’ pursuit of strategic goals, such as improved public perception or neutralized political and civil society opposition, sometimes leads to the dissemination of content that is misleading or false (Brulle et al. 2021). Here, once again, the fossil fuel industry is in the fore: an analysis of print advertorials from ExxonMobil in The New York Times between 1989-2004 showed that the advertorials overwhelmingly “expressed doubt about climate change as real and human-caused, serious, and solvable, whereas peer-reviewed papers and internal reports authored by company employees by and large did not” (Supran and Oreskes 2020: abstract).

This article’s focus is on a direct descendant of the advertorial, adapted to digital media. Native advertising is paid content presented in a form (in terms of placement, header, style, font) similar to the “native” content of its host site: that is, on a news website, news articles. If Mobil Oil’s advertorials were intended to blur the line between paid corporate messaging and editor-vetted opinion statements, native advertising elides the opinion step altogether and insinuates corporate copy as news itself (AUTHOR in press).

Our topical focus is the fossil fuel industry, which as just noted is well known for both its engagement with integrated content and its dissemination of false and misleading messages, especially about the environment and climate change. Given the sparsity of existing work in this particular area, our aims are both descriptive and analytic: first, we wish to ascertain the extent to which the fossil fuel industry is using native advertising to convey its messages to the public. How widespread is the practice within major English-language news outlets? Second, when they engage in native advertising, what messages do they prioritize? What are they using native advertising to say?
News media and native advertising

By the twentieth century, funding of news media in the English-speaking world has been predominantly commercial, financed by the sale of advertisements (most completely in the United States; Hallin and Mancini 2004; Starr 2004). As is well known to readers of this journal, the dual-product mission of news media (to simultaneously produce informative citizen-oriented news, and provide audiences to advertisers) was always fraught, but during the “high modern” era managed to strike a tenuous balance thanks to a combination of professional norms and civically-minded media owners protected by monopoly market conditions. Insulating the civic products of journalism from the influence of advertiser pressure and other business interests has been a longstanding priority (Kovach & Rosenstiel 2001).

However, changes that are technological, political, cultural, and economic are upending this formula (Baym 2009; Picard 2020). Of primary concern to this discussion is the implosion of the advertising-centered business model that has news organizations scraping and experimenting for new ways to support their basic functions. Hence the proliferation of innovative new forms of advertising and sponsorship within the media.

This is where native advertising comes in: as noted above, native ads mimic the format of news articles, thereby often evading audiences’ growing resistance to conventional forms of digital advertising. The advantage for advertisers is obvious. Advertisers have always paid for association with a news product held in (historically) high esteem. But better than providing a place for advertising next to the news, native advertising promises the opportunity to insert commercial messages as news itself. When a sponsor’s message serves not only a commercial purpose but also seeks to sway public opinion or political discourse, native advertising is an especially attractive option (Brulle et al. 2020). And sponsors are willing to pay top dollar for native ads precisely because they are difficult to distinguish from news articles. Between October 2020 and October 2023, just seven leading US news outlets were paid over $46 million to create native ads for the fossil fuel industry (AUTHOR in press).

It is therefore no surprise that struggling news organizations have embraced the practice. In fact, much of today’s native advertising—and most of our sample—is now crafted by employees of news organizations themselves, via in-house content studios. These studios perform the functions of traditional advertising agencies—though news organizations are often careful to note that it is not their journalists writing the copy (AUTHOR in press; Einstein 2016).

Yet, alongside the revenue they generate, native ads raise a number of concerns about their effects on readers, news organizations’ credibility, and the independence of reporting. Studies consistently find that a large majority of readers do not recognize the difference between the paid posts and genuine journalistic articles, even when government-mandated disclosures are present (Amazeen et al. 2025; Amazeen and Wojdynski 2020; Wojdynski and Evans 2016). Although we don’t know enough about how journalists and editors feel about native advertising, existing work shows they are aware of its deceptive nature (Schauster et al. 2016), pointing to possible morale implications. Moreover, studies of native advertising indicate that when it is shared on social media, disclosures identifying the content as commercial often disappear (Amazeen and Vargo 2021; An, Kang and Koo 2019). For example, when shared on Twitter, a native ad in The Washington Post sponsored by the American Petroleum Institute appears exactly like a Post news article.

Finally, at least one study has raised concerns that native advertising buys may affect editorial decision-making: Vargo and Amazeen (2021) found that native campaigns were associated with reduced subsequent news coverage of the sponsors. This is especially concerning given native advertising’s attractiveness for political, as opposed to purely commercial purposes, and the evidence that an outlet’s genuine news coverage may contradict claims made in sponsors’ advertising (Supran and Oreskes 2020), in essence offering competing news agendas (Vargo and Amazeen 2021) reminiscent of the Mobil Oil advertorials from decades ago.
Fossil fuels, climate and disinformation

As fossil fuel companies increasingly communicate on the topic of climate change, these concerns are well founded. Research has documented both “top-down” disinformation (from politicians and corporations, e.g. Oreskes and Supran 2011) and “bottom-up” disinformation (from online networks, e.g. Lamb et al. 2020). Particularly on the issue of the scientific consensus about anthropogenic warming, corporate and political actors worked systematically and scientifically beginning in the 1980s to mislead the public and neutralize efforts to limit carbon dioxide emissions (Oreskes and Conway 2011).

With media and congressional scrutiny of the fossil fuel industry’s influence on climate change, the industry’s investments in advertising have grown. According to Brulle, Aronczyk, and Carmichael (2020: 88), fossil fuel advertising “is a dominant strategy to manipulate environmental discourse and influence political outcomes around climate change.” Between 1986 and 2015, the five largest fossil fuel companies in the US together spent an average of $120 million annually on advertising (Brulle et al. 2020). Between the Paris Agreement in 2015 and 2018, the world’s five largest oil companies collectively spent $195 million per year on advertising campaigns.

Over the years, the focus of advertisements by the fossil fuel industry has evolved. Prior to the 1980s, there was little concern about environmental issues in advertising messages. However, with the emergence in the 1970s of the US Environmental Protection Agency and environmental regulations, this began to change (Vos 2014). From the late 1980s until the mid-2000s, advertisements from the oil industry explicitly cast doubt on the scientific evidence of climate change (Bonneuil, Choquet and Franta 2021; Farrell et al. 2019;), typically employing a strategic framing that researchers have labeled “scientific uncertainty” (Supran and Oreskes 2021: 712). For instance, one 1997 ad claimed, “The science of climate change is too uncertain to mandate a plan of action that could plunge economies into turmoil.”

Since the mid-2000s, that narrative has shifted to implicit acknowledgement using discourses that express anthropogenic global warming as a “risk” but redirecting responsibility away from the industry and onto individual consumers while asserting a continuing need for fossil fuels in the future (Supran and Oreskes 2021: 712). For example, a 2008 ad from ExxonMobil stated, “To meet this demand, while addressing the risks posed by rising greenhouse gas emissions, we’ll need to call upon [a] broad mix of energy sources” (Supran and Oreskes 2021: 704). Similarly, between 2004-2006, a series of ads from BP implored consumers to “Reduce your carbon footprint…”
Fossil fuel companies and narratives about climate change

In recent years, there is growing consensus that these “discourses of climate delay,” (Lamb et al. 2020) have become predominant, at least in the United States and United Kingdom. These types of messages acknowledge the existence of climate change but rationalize inaction or insufficient measures; they capitalize on debates about what actions should be taken, the pace of those actions, who is responsible, and how costs and benefits should be distributed (Bohr 2016; Jacques and Knox 2016; McKie 2019). The discourses tap into very real anxieties as societies confront the climate crisis and the changes that genuinely addressing the crisis would entail, but they shift into delay tactics when they distort rather than clarify or suggest that taking action is an insurmountable challenge.

One analysis from Lamb and colleagues (2020) establishes a typology with four categories of common features that distinguish climate delay discourses: redirecting responsibility, pushing non-transformative solutions, emphasizing the downsides of climate policy, or surrendering to climate change. Discourses that “redirect responsibility” (Lamb et al. 2020: 3) sidestep accountability for addressing climate change. While these narratives acknowledge the difficulty of creating a fair and holistic response, they frequently set unattainable conditions for action, suggesting that others must act first before we do—thus evading immediate opportunities for climate action and policy. Discourses that “push non-transformative solutions,” meanwhile, advocate for ineffective climate measures, diverting focus from more impactful and meaningful actions, instead prioritizing limited definitions of success, optimistic framing, and entrepreneurial values over transformative initiatives and binding regulations. Alternatively, discourses that “emphasize the downsides” (Lamb et al. 2020: 4) of climate action deny or dismiss the potential for creating inclusive policies that offer social benefits and gain broad support. They focus on the negatives of climate action, suggesting that these drawbacks impose a heavier burden on society than the impacts of not taking action (Coan et al. 2021). Finally, discourses that “surrender” (Lamb et al. 2020: 4) to climate change cast doubt on the feasibility of mitigation, highlighting what appear to be insurmountable political, social, or biophysical obstacles. These narratives imply that mitigation efforts are pointless and propose that adaptation is the only viable response, sometimes framed in religious terms as leaving our fate in “God’s hands” (Lamb et al. 2020: 5).

Three other types of discourse that have been identified are misdirection, climate silence and greenwashing. Indeed, despite climate catastrophes playing out around the globe, social media posts from fossil fuel companies generally do not acknowledge the crises as they play out (Supran and Hickey 2022). More common are narratives of misdirection and climate silence. For Supran and Hickey (2022: 3), misdirection involves “engaging [in] topics unrelated to companies’ core business operations,” such as when a company highlights their engagement with fashion, social causes, or sports. In so doing, this bestows cultural capital and validates fossil fuel interests’ license to operate, deflects attention away from their advancement of the climate crisis, and thus creates more favorable perceptions of these brands. Climate silence can occur alongside misdirection or other discourses, being the lack of acknowledgement or mention of the climate crisis (Supran and Hickey 2022).

“Greenwashing,” a term first coined by activist Jay Westerveld in 1986 (Cherry and Sneirson 2012: 140), refers to narratives that portray companies as environmentally aware and committed to low-carbon technologies or technological advancements, when in fact their investments, practices, and policy actions show otherwise. (Supran and Hickey 2022).

The preceding analyses of narratives reveal a shift in fossil fuel interests’ social media strategies, moving away from directly addressing climate change and fossil interests’ role in it, toward strategic brand positioning through language and imagery that promote green, innovative, and charitable identities. Moreover, the increased use of experts and futuristic, scientific visuals promote a “Green Innovation” narrative (Supran and Hickey 2022: 48) that aligns with fossil fuel industries' history of employing perceived experts to legitimize their public stances on scientific issues.
Research questions

It is into this nexus that we place the present study. A good deal is known about fossil fuel companies’ promotions around the issue of climate change; but to date, studies analyzing the content of fossil fuel industry advertisements have focused primarily on print (e.g., Murphree and Aucoin 2010; St. John 2014; Stanford-McIntyre 2017; Supran and Oreskes 2020; 2021) and social media advertising (Supran and Hickey 2022). We know of no existing research on how companies are using native advertising to communicate about climate change and mitigation. And given the evidence that fossil fuel companies are leveraging native advertising to greenwash their image (Author in press), more scrutiny into the nature, extent, and effects of this practice is warranted.​

In this study, we explore how fossil fuel interests are using native advertising to communicate about energy and climate change, the narratives they prioritize, and how we should understand the tension news organizations face between the revenue native advertising can generate and its potentially misleading consequences. Our research questions ask: RQ1) To what extent are fossil fuel interests using native advertising to communicate about energy and climate? RQ2) When they do so, what narratives are prioritized? Especially, do we see evidence of climate denialism, or are native ads used to promote narratives more like greenwashing, misdirection, silence and delay? Finally, RQ3) how should we understand the tension news organizations face between the revenue native advertising provides and its potentially misleading consequences?
METHOD
To answer these questions, we combine human content analysis of latent content features with automated text analysis of manifest language use (primarily unigram and bigram word occurrences).
Constructing the dataset

One of the challenges of studying native advertising is the difficulty of extracting content from news sites at scale (Author in press). We built a large corpus of native advertisements through several steps, advancing the work of Vargo and Amazeen (2021). This article presents results from the subset that were sponsored by fossil fuel companies or trade groups. We started from a list of the 50 English-language news websites with the most traffic in the United States. From the list, we selected sites that (a) produced original news content, i.e., were not only news aggregators; and (b) contained native advertising in some form. Native advertising was operationalized as advertisements that were assigned their own url (i.e., were not banner ads) and were generally formatted in the style of news articles on the site (i.e., contained the news organization’s logo as a header, and reflected typical formatting of headlines, font, paragraph structure, etc.) Twenty six websites met these initial criteria.

We next examined each site to identify reliable indicators of native advertising for automated collection. This required customization to each website, sometimes relying upon keywords present on the page (e.g., the phrase “paid post,”), sometimes website structure (e.g. the presence of “sponsorcontent” in a particular position within the URL), and often a combination of the two. We also collated a list of 77 keywords related to energy and/or the environment. This allowed us to combine site-specific indicators of native advertising with each of the keywords in a series of queries using Google Dork. For example, for The New York Times, we found that the term “paidpost” occurs in every native ad’s URL. Our queries for the Times thus took the form “Site:nytimes.com/paidpost TERM” with TERM iterating over each of the search keywords. For each unique URL returned in the search, we used custom python scrapers to extract text and metadata. This process resulted in a collection of thousands of native advertisements from a wide array of sponsors, from health care firms to green energy companies. However, despite customizing our query to each site, we found that it was not possible to reliably identify native advertising on several sites and dropped them from the sample.

Finally, we identified the set of fossil fuel companies and trade associations present as sponsors in our data and extracted their ads as our final dataset. Our final dataset consists of 252 native ads, each sponsored by one of eleven companies and trade groups, published in one of eleven news outlets. We did not restrict the date ranges of advertisements that we collected; the dates of advertisements in our data correspond to what is known about the rise of native advertising (Einstein 2016): the dates range from 2014 until the time we collected the data in the fall of 2022. Further investigation (additional custom searches) turned up no further ads, so we consider the ads in our dataset to be comprehensive of the ads published by the companies and outlets in our sample—at least those that were available at the time of data collection in fall 2022 (a result of the use of several keywords extremely common in fossil fuel advertising; see Appendix).
Human coding

The core of our analysis explored advertisements’ mentions of environmental issues, claims about environmental records, and themes related to the world’s uses of energy. These relatively latent features were coded by humans. Our codebook was based on prior research of fossil fuel companies’ communications (discussed above; especially Coan et al. 2022; Lamb et al. 2020; Supran and Hickey 2022; Supran and Oreskes 2021) as well as preliminary investigations of the data.

First, given the fossil fuel industry’s long history of misinformation and obfuscation about the science of climate, as well as avoiding the topic (“climate silence”), two codes examined the presence of discussions of climate science specifically, and environmental issues in general:

climate_science measured mentions of the mechanisms, causes or effects of climate change–i.e., a mere mention of the words “climate change” was sufficient for this code. If climate_science was present, the coder further assessed whether the discussion was (a) consistent with the scientific consensus or (b) presented skepticism of the consensus.
enviro_issue was more general, requiring mention of an environmental issue, such as climate change, pollution, sustainability, etc.

Supran and Hickey (2022) also pointed out ways in which companies over promise the environmental benefits of their practices–or intended future practices (“greenwashing”). Thus, to explore companies’ contentions that their work was in line with improved environmental performance we created the following codes:
enviro_improve assessed whether companies were asserting that their environmental record was improving.

In addition to discourses directly about environmental issues and companies’ practices, scholars have noted discourses that emphasize the contributions fossil fuel energy makes to quality of life (Coan et al. 2022; Lamb et al. 2020). Thus:
need_for_power assessed whether a given ad highlighted society’s need for power (usually in industrialized societies).
developing_countries looked at whether an ad pointed out the benefits of gaining power to a developing society.

Along the same lines, and in line with Supran and Hickey’s (2022) “misdirection,” we assessed whether an ad mentioned benefits society gains from the company’s operations beyond the direct use of power and derivative products (e.g. plastics):
other_benefits. This included benefits such as economic stimulus, as well as the company’s charity programs, scholarships, community work, etc.
Finally, we drew on three of Lamb and colleagues’ (2020) varieties of discourses to draw attention away from companies’ practices for our final three codes:
foreign_problem measured efforts to redirect attention to pollution happening in other countries (drawing on Lamb et al.’s “whataboutism”).
individual_action looked at promotions of individual action as the solution to environmental problems (Lamb et al.’s “individualism”).
doomism measured engaging in “doomism” or surrender (Lamb et al.)—the fatalistic attitude that environmental harm was unavoidable or that climate change could not be halted.

Two coders were trained and applied the codebook to text and infographics from the advertisements. To keep the coding task manageable, coders examined the first 3000 characters of each advertisement–about 400 words–intended to give a good indication of the major themes of the ad. When available, the coders coded directly from the live URL, and thus coded text stored in infographics that might have been missed by our scrapers; when the URL was no longer available they coded the text we had collected.

The coders conducted a reliability check on 41 randomly-selected advertisements (16% of the collection). Table 1 displays the percent agreement and Krippendorff’s alpha for the codes. The ten main codes were each present/absent, while the climate_science subcode had two categories (a = consistent with the scientific consensus; b = a skeptical view of the scientific consensus). The statistics are generally acceptable (Krippendorff’s alpha above .7) for relatively latent codes in a new research area. After the reliability check, differences in the subsample were resolved through discussion, and one coder coded the remainder of the data.

Automated text analysis

We complement human coding with simple and highly manifest automated text analysis, mainly bigrams; bigrams are often used in text analysis and interpretation for their straightforwardness and better interpretability than individual word occurrences (Angus, Bruns and Tan 2023). Text analysis was performed on the same dataset as the human coders analyzed, with the minor exceptions that (a) whereas human coders considered text in graphics our scrapers could not collect, the automated analyses did not; and (b) the automated analyses only considered advertisements for which we were able to obtain at least twenty tokens (words; we retained 87.7% of the original sample). In conducting the automated analyses, we tokenized each text and removed punctuation and stopwords.
RESULTS
Mentions of the environment and climate change

We begin with concerns about the practice of leaving environmental concerns out of communications altogether (i.e., “climate silence”; Supran and Hickey 2022). Our collection of 252 native advertisements makes clear that native ads are frequently used by fossil fuel companies and trade groups to communicate about the environment and climate (RQ1): a substantial majority (75%) of our advertisements featured environmental concerns (enviro_issue). A bigram analysis bears this out, with the most-frequently occurring ten bigrams being natural_gas, oil_gas, climate_change, r_d, renewable_energy, greenhouse_gas, energy_efficiency, energy_mix, net_zero and global_energy.

However, though environmental issues were regularly presented to readers, the science of climate change’s mechanisms and effects (climate_science)–was very sparse, occurring in only 20 advertisements (7.9%). Quite simply, the science of climate was taken for granted in the vast majority of the ads: in those few cases where we detected mentions of climate science, the science mentioned was always consistent with the scientific consensus, and it was not portrayed as uncertain (100% received climate_science subcode a).

Our second research question (RQ2) inquired into the types of narratives prioritized. We present those narratives in order of prevalence. Beyond mere mentions of environmental issues, most of the advertisements (63%) asserted that the sponsoring company was improving its environmental record (enviro_improve). How they claimed to do so, however, is a further question. If we look again at frequently-occurring bigrams (in terms of occurrence in the most ads), we can compare ads that contain assertions of environmental improvement to those that did not (Table 2).

Not surprisingly, terms directly related to environmental issues (“greenhouse gas, “climate change”) are much more prevalent in ads that assert environmental improvements; these ads are acknowleding a problem and claiming to be part of its solution. Less obvious is why “natural gas” should be the most prevalent bigram in ads about improving environmental records (and more prevalent than in ads not making that claim). The answer is that when companies touted their improving environmental record, it was often by describing a turn to natural gas as an environmentally-friendly fuel source. Total Energies engaged in this type of discourse frequently. One illustration is an ad in CNBC headlined “Total and Natural Gas: A Deliberate Stance in a Changing Global Energy Landscape.” In it, Total states that they have increased their production of natural gas, and that this has both economic and environmental benefits. Specifically, the ad compares natural gas favorably to coal, and even comparable to renewable sources. One sub-headline states, “Lower CO2 emission and complementary to renewable energies.”

Assessing this kind of message in terms of greenwashing is somewhat nuanced. On one hand, the message fits within Lamb et al’s (2020) category of “non-transformative” solutions: it implies that fossil fuel companies on their own are transitioning to a lower-carbon future–through another fossil fuel. At the same time, natural gas is widely recognized as less carbon intensive than other forms of fossil fuel (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2021). We should also note that our data collection period coincided with an unprecedented boom in natural gas production made possible by innovations in drilling technologies (U.S. Energy Information Administration, n.d.), meaning that the “turn” to natural gas was primarily a product of technological development, not environmental concern.
Unproven technologies and misleading initiatives

Given the dominant position of environmental improvement narratives in our data, it is worth taking a further useful step, recognizing that different companies promote different environmental initiatives. Once again, we employ a combination of human coding and bigram analyses, by comparing the five most prevalent bigrams in advertisements claiming environmental improvement across the sponsoring companies (see Appendix for full table). This answers the question, when companies are promoting their environmental improvements, what do they point to?

What we see is that many companies’ top bigrams reflect the larger pattern in the data. (For example, Total’s are “natural_gas,” “r_d,” “energy_efficiency,” “energy_mix,” and “oil_gas.”) Exxon’s stand out, however, for their distinctive naming of (so far unproven or undeveloped) technologies: “carbon_capture,” “capture_storage,” “carbon_footprint,” “renewable_diesel,” “blue_hydrogen.”

For example, Figure 1 shows a native advertisement in the Wall Street Journal from Exxon touting blue hydrogen. “Blue hydrogen is a low-carbon fuel produced from natural gas in combination with carbon capture and storage (CCS),” the ad explains. “This clean-burning fuel produces zero CO2 when combusted, meaning it can play a vital role in a lower-emission future.”

However, this technology is unproven at scale: the ad itself is all about “plans.” Moreover, evidence is accumulating suggesting that blue hydrogen–which Exxon proposes to create by burning natural gas and capturing the CO2 emissions–is neither a clean energy source nor economically viable (Howarth and Jacobson 2021), facts noted by at least one legacy news outlet.

Another example from ExxonMobil promoted technologies that we know to have been unproven—because Exxon abandoned it in 2022. The ad, still available on the New York Times website, promoted ExxonMobil’s research on algae as a potential source of carbon-neutral biofuels. It is now well-known because several state attorneys general have cited it in lawsuits against ExxonMobil for misleading claims: Massachusetts’ suit against ExxonMobil notes that this ad “misleadingly gushes about [ExxonMobil’s] efforts to develop energy production from alternate sources like algae and plant waste, efforts that pale in comparison to the investment ExxonMobil continues to make in fossil fuel production” (Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. ExxonMobil: 169-171).

Once again, like the mention of natural gas above, evaluating the veracity of these claims is complex. On one hand, the specific claims being made by Exxon are, as far as we can tell, true. On the other hand, they elide the critical context that the technologies are unproven and may never materialize: context that good news reporting would—and has—included (and that may have legal ramifications).

For our purposes here, what is most important is to recognize these discourses as positioning fossil fuel companies as the solution: as “innovators” dedicated to meeting energy needs sustainably. We might call these narratives “unproven technologies” and categorize them as sub-sets of Lamb and colleagues’ (2020: 2) “fossil fuel solutionism,” itself a subvariety of pushing for non-transformative solutions.
Reminders of the importance of energy

Scholars have also noted the tactic of emphasizing society’s need for energy as an excuse for continued reliance on fossil fuels. We detected these discourses, most prominently in the form of mentions of the public’s need for power (need_for_power), which was present in 29% of ads. Narratives present in these ads often featured renewables and alternative fuel sources, but also contained arguments that traditional (fossil) fuel sources will continue to be needed to meet energy demands. For example, an ad sponsored by the American Petroleum Institute in the Washington Post in 2019 took a seemingly positive stance toward renewable and alternative fuel sources but also cautioned against a rapid move away from fossil sources (see Figure 2). It named natural gas and other traditional fuel sources as necessities to meet growing energy demands:

U.S. energy demand is expected to increase by about 13 percent by 2050. Given these realities, complete dependence on renewables may be out of reach. Even decades into the future, utilities will remain reliant on a mix of resources, including natural gas, to achieve a sustainable energy landscape.

The ad also highlighted the “limitations of renewables,” suggesting that they are unreliable: “The biggest challenge of renewables is their intermittent nature…Consumers large and small need and expect a steady and reliable source of electricity.” Claims that renewables are unreliable have been directly contradicted by news reports from the Washington Post’s own environmental reporter, again demonstrating the misleading nature of some of the native advertisements (RQ3).

While this finding is consistent with Supran and Oreskes’ (2021) finding that past Exxon advertisements have sought to individualize responsibility for climate action, we did not find that this discourse was as explicit as recommending individual actions, such as recycling or driving an electric car (individual_action; we found only a single instance—0.4% of ads).

Companies also promoted benefits they provide communities that go beyond direct uses of energy and products derived from fossil fuels (other_benefits). A fifth (19.4%) of the ads described how fossil fuel companies foster economic growth and business development, support local production, provide job opportunities, and engage in charity work such as building schools and sending girls to school. For example, Chevron ran a campaign in The Atlantic in 2014 that highlighted the natural gas industry’s economic benefits in Appalachia. “Now, as in other parts of Appalachian coal country, Connellsville is experiencing a resurgence as the energy industry moves back into the region to tap the vast supply of shale gas in the underground Marcellus formation,” the ad states. “As a result, the median household income in Connellsville’s Fayette County has ballooned nearly 42 percent from $27,451 in 2000 to $38,903 last year, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.” Supran and Hickey (2022) categorize these types of messages as misdirection, but in the context of our study, its relatively small prevalence must be placed in comparison to the much larger set of ads that mentioned environmental concerns.

Whereas discussions of the public’s need for energy tended to focus on developed countries, a handful of ads also emphasized how lives in developing countries are improving as a result of gaining access to energy (our developing_countries code, present in 6.3% of ads). A good number of these ads were from Total Energies, which used eleven ads to describe the challenges faced by societies with limited energy access, such as lack of electricity for water pumps, sewage treatment plants, schools and hospitals. Interestingly, a number of these ads either don’t mention Total’s efforts to provide energy in developing countries, or do so in an opaque way–for example by mentioning a nonprofit organization funded by Total.
Redirecting responsibility

A final set of discourses relate to what Lamb et al. (2020) called “redirecting responsibility.” We identified two forms. The first were narratives mentioning the power use, energy/fuel demand, energy/fuel imports, carbon emissions, or other environmental harms originating in countries other than the United States, Canada, or Europe, including the UK or Russia (which we presumed to be the companies’ primary markets). This message (our other_countries code) was present in 12.3% of ads in our data, and we observed that the common trend among native ads was to identify another country that is a source of environmental harm, and then the company presents itself as part of the solution. For example, in an ad sponsored by Ceraweek and published in the Wall Street Journal in 2018, Ceraweek highlights China’s growing pollution problem as an effect of its rapid economic growth and positions itself as part of the solution to provide a clean fuel source that will meet environmental goals and energy demand.
DISCUSSION

This study, the first to comprehensively document native advertising by fossil fuel companies, has characterized and quantified the narratives appearing in native ads. Our results show consistency with varieties of climate delay narratives described in recent research on other communication media, though the particular distribution of narratives that we saw in native ads probably represents that medium’s generally positive and aspirational, and possibly factual, tone.

Contrary to concerns about “climate silence,” the ads mentioned the environment and climate change regularly–and did so largely to show that fossil fuel companies have the issue well in hand and are well on the way to providing solutions. In comparison, other discourses that have been described in other contexts were less present, though a quarter of ads did advance reminders of energy’s role in powering modern life and a fifth promoted benefits of fossil fuel products beyond energy. The subtext that “disruptive change is not necessary” (Lamb et al. 2020) was strong, and the irony of an industry’s turn from denying the existence of a problem it had a primary hand in creating, to promoting itself as that problem’s solution, is evident.

Our particular sample and method also helpful us to uncover a sub-narrative relating to the presentation of low-carbon initiatives: unproven technologies. We suspect, again, that the advertising context, well known for aspirational language, is a place companies may be likely to direct this kind of communication.
Is it disinformation?

We have focused on documenting the varieties of claims themselves, and only commenting on their veracity when existing evidence was already available. We did see a number of claims that refer to seemingly substantive technology that when scrutinized by journalists or researchers, seem aspirational at best if not misleading. Future research might further grapple with this question by, first, quantifying the set of aspirational technologies that prove infeasible (such as Exxon's forays into algae, above), and second, examining in more detail how readers interpret such hopeful statements.

In addition, the truth value of many of the statements we saw are highly dependent on context–in this case, the context of the climate crisis–making straightforward claims of “misinformation” difficult. Surely the vast majority of claims we saw were true on their face: natural gas does emit substantially less carbon dioxide per unit energy produced than coal; many of the estimates of growing future energy are probably reasonable. But in the context of the scale of the problem our societies face, contrasting one fossil fuel against another may be a form of invalid comparison.
Native advertising and the press

Our results also raise further questions about the role of native advertising in supporting institutions of the press. This is especially highlighted by the fact that claims contained in the native advertisements were sometimes contradictory to what was being reported from the journalists in the newsroom. For instance, while the New York Times’ T Brand Studio produced native advertising for ExxonMobil promoting its biofuel initiatives to portray the company as environmentally responsible, its newsroom uncovered that the company’s energy-wasting practices were on the rise. Similarly, the Washington Post produced native advertising for the American Petroleum Institute, asserting that fossil fuels are still a crucial energy source due to the unreliability of renewable energy—a claim contradicted by the Post's own climate coverage. It is in this way that numerous well-known news outlets are creating advertising content for major oil and gas companies, lending the industry a sense of credibility as they present misleading climate claims to unsuspecting readers (Author in press; Supran and Oreskes 2020).

Moreover, publishers are often contractually obligated to not only create the content and distribute it on their news sites and applications, but also to amplify the content on their social media properties to achieve predetermined metrics of “likes” and shares (AUTHOR in press; Sirrah 2022). As previously mentioned, when this content is shared on social media, the federally required disclosure labels often disappear (Amazeen and Vargo 2021; An, Kang and Koo 2019), leaving the appearance that a news article is being shared rather than advertising. Undisclosed native advertising is also showing up in Google search results (AUTHOR in press). Furthermore, corporate sponsors such as Shell and Chevron can repurpose the native advertisements to use as “media artifacts” and transfer them for use across the digital ecosystem, complete with news site branding to confer legitimacy (McAllister, Cikovic and Salomone 2023: 305). What is actually a commercial message appears to be a news article from a leading news outlet that can be used to influence public opinion and policy makers. Yet, how these native ads travel throughout the media ecosystem – particularly those having to do with climate issues – has not been studied and warrants future research.

It is also important to note that our conceptualization and sample has taken place in only English-language news media, from only two countries (though indeed many of the outlets in our sample have global reach). It is important that future research consider how these dynamics are playing out in other countries, with differently-organized media systems, and in other languages.
Conclusion

We have great sympathy for news organizations struggling to remain solvent in the digital era. Still, the layered ways in which native advertising can deceive readers–first, whether it is advertising at all, and second, in its misleading or mis-interpretable claims–strike at the heart of journalism’s primary mission to inform its consumers. This is obviously a significant conversation the field of journalism needs to have (and is having). We do wonder, given the sometimes divergent claims of native ads and newsrooms, whether ads should be subject to some degree of journalistic scrutiny. If they are trading on the news organization’s own credibility, should the news organization not exercise some degree of authority on their content?

At a time of desperately low trust in journalism (Newman et al. 2023), but when the public should be turning to traditional news sources for accurate, vetted information, we are concerned that news publishers may add to the confusion and erode their own legitimacy by blurring commercial and journalistic content with the use of native advertising. In this case, the misinformation may not be as loud and blatant as the disinformation that grabs headlines from social media–and often its misleadingness is a delicate matter of context–but given its placement within our society’s most recognizable news outlets, and its reach to some of our society’s most privileged citizens, its impact should not be underestimated–or understudied.
